The Hex Update: Issue 047

the hex update
media
The future of TV advertising–attribution; Why creator content belongs in an AI strategy; TV size and geography for targetting; and some other cool things I came across this week
Author

Collin K. Berke, Ph.D.

November 23, 2026

Let’s catch up

Friends of the internet, welcome to Issue 047. Solid week this week; I was able to tick a few things off my to-do list. I also was able to sharpen the axe, where I tidied up some areas of my work that needed some better organization. If the holiday season is a time where things slow down, maybe you to can take some time to sharpen your axe.

So anyways, let’s learn.

Three things

Here’s what caught my attention this week:

Televisionation—Friday Fireside: Scott Weisenthal, Global Head of Marketing and Insights at Comcast Advertising (podcast)

Here’s a conversation with Scott Weisenthal, Global Head of Marketing and Insights at Comcast Advertising. Several points in this interview caught my attention: the gap between big brands and smaller businesses to use TV advertising; connecting the pieces of a media buy–including attribution; the importance of shared experiences and word-of-mouth; and Answer Engine Optimization. I’m walking away with several quotes from this interview. Here are two that caught my attention:

Shared experiences are what create culture. (10M55S)

LLMs are word-of-mouth on steroids. (14M06S)

Why creator content belongs in your AI search strategy (blog)

The main point of this article is clear: creator content is critical to an AI search strategy. It was staggering to read that 82% of AI citations come from earned media. Video was mentioned to play a critical role as well, especially long-format YouTube videos. As quoted in the article about video:

Popularity doesn’t predict citation value, structure does.

The article also included some points about the value of social conversations.

Wolk’s Week in Review: Can V Really Shake Up TV Measurement? (blog)

This post provides some opinions on the current measurement differences between linear, connected TV, and digital measurement. It discusses a new system to address this called VIP (Verified Inch Price), which bases advertising inventory sales on the size of a TV and the demographics a city the TV is located. This quote from the article caught my attention:

TV is never going to have the granularity of digital, no matter how many algorithms we try and force on it.

The article’s stance is TV is a branding vehicle, it’s a shared device, and as such it doesn’t need the same level of granularity as digital. The value of VIP here is the simplicity it provides for ad buyers.

Check out the links above for the full story in each item, not just my brief summary and analysis.

What I found interesting this week

This week, I spent some time reading and learning more about Google Dataform’s workspaces. I started to learn more about what workspaces are, how to set one up, and all the features that are available. I also learned more about the initialization process, which included exploring more about the purpose of the following directories and files for a project:

  • definitions/
  • includes/
  • workflow_settings.yaml

I also spent some more time understanding more about SQLX and JavaScript files and how they can be used to help define workflows. I’m drafting a blog post with some notes about what I learned, so that will be up soon.
